article.articleHeadline: UN hails progress in Ebola response, cites insecurity as biggest challenge
article.articleSummary:
- Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) reaches six months since mid-May declaration, with confirmed cases surpassing 11,100 and deaths over 5,400, making it the second-worst Ebola outbreak on record. The Bundibugyo virus drives transmission across eight provinces in east, central and west Congo, now spreading to more rural, hard-to-reach areas. No approved treatments or vaccines exist for Bundibugyo Ebola. Children account for more than one-third of deaths, with up to 500 new cases weekly. - WHO reports 11,000 Ebola infections and 5,400 deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, six months after the outbreak was declared a public health emergency. About one third of fatalities are children. Urban foci have been contained and hospital occupancy reduced to roughly 50%, but community transmission persists in rural, isolated areas with 400–500 new cases weekly. Insecurity, including more than 80 armed attacks on health workers and facilities, hampers response efforts. Three experimental antiviral treatments have entered clinical trials, and two new vaccine candidates are expected in the coming weeks. - Ebola continues to spread in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), UN Senior Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis said on 14 November 2026, despite significant progress against the outbreak over the past six months and spread to new areas. Continued transmission requires sustained efforts and stronger on-the-ground measures to contain the outbreak. Harneis outlined three operational priorities, including ensuring safe and unhindered access to affected areas, a key challenge as violence in parts of eastern DRC hampers response and contact tracing. He stressed that violence in recent days has killed more people than Ebola, highlighting the need to address security and humanitarian access as part of outbreak response.
- An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo prompts a new U.S. travel health measure announced by the U.S. Embassy in Peru on 2026-11-03. To prevent international spread via commercial air travel, the CDC requires all passengers flying to the United States or transiting through it to confirm they have not visited the DRC in the preceding 21 days. Airlines will collect a sworn declaration from each passenger at check-in or before boarding, in either physical or electronic form. The policy is described as preventive. The World Health Organization reports more than 11,100 confirmed Ebola cases and about 5,433 deaths over six months, with recent cases detected in Kenya and Nigeria indicating border risk. article.articleHeadline: Silent TB in India: 1.5 million asymptomatic infections.

- In India, a nationwide TB campaign uncovering about 1.5 million asymptomatic infections underscores the burden of silent tuberculosis. The Ministry of Health reported 14.97 million asymptomatic cases among 48.64 million newly detected infections from 7 Dec 2024 to 8 Nov 2026, after screening over 250 million people. Silent (subclinical) TB is active bacterial disease confirmed by laboratory tests or radiographic changes, yet lacking common symptoms such as chronic cough, night sweats, fever, weight loss, or chest pain. - India reduced TB mortality by 38% since 2015, per the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2026, outpacing the global 35% decline and achieving a 94% treatment success rate. César Neves, Secretary of State of Health, urges continued prevention through elimination of breeding sites even during lulls. The initiative seeks to curb transmission by engaging communities ahead of peak transmission periods linked to climate shifts from El Niño, addressing ongoing risks in Paraná.

article.articleHeadline: Uncertainty over the Yellow Fever vaccine shortage.
article.articleSummary: Yellow fever vaccine shortage hits pharmacies in Buenos Aires as the 2026 summer season nears. Free vaccination ended in 2025, making the dose mandatory for entry to many Latin American destinations, with stock exhausted in Buenos Aires hospitals by mid-2026 and inoculation shifting to private purchase. The national Health Ministry limited free access to high-risk regions, raising equity concerns for travelers and public health. In practice, pharmacies report widespread shortages, with some outlets carrying minimal stock or operating on order; vaccination requires official training to administer and issue the certificate. In La Plata, only about 50–60 of 330 pharmacies have completed the course. Each dose costs over 300,000 pesos, potentially exceeding 1 million pesos for a four-person family. Endemic zones (Bolivia, Peru, Colombia, Paraguay, Cuba, Panama, Venezuela, parts of Brazil) require the certificate; some northern Argentine provinces (Misiones, Corrientes, Formosa, Salta, Jujuy, Chaco) still offer free doses.

article.articleHeadline: Cardiac arrest due to Chagas disease led to the death of a female passenger on a flight from Brasília to Porto Velho.
article.articleSummary: A 76-year-old woman, Nair Carrier Dinis, died on a Brasília-to-Porto Velho flight from cardiac arrest linked to Chagas disease. The death, confirmed by Brasília’s SVO, was attributed to chronic chagasic cardiomyopathy caused by Trypanosoma cruzi infection, with the death certificate citing a mixed shock (cardiogenic, distributive, hemorrhagic, obstructive) following the arrest. Passengers reported nose and mouth bleeding after takeoff; onboard volunteers performed CPR for about 20 minutes before declaring death. The aircraft departed Brasília at 21:30 on Sunday the 8th, circled, then returned, with FlightAware listing a 46-minute flight. The body arrived Porto Velho the night of the 11th, was transported ~200 km to Ariquemes (RO) for wake beginning at 5:00 on the 12th, and burial started around 9:30. Documents found included a history of chagasic cardiomegaly and megacolon and a cardiovascular medication prescription, indicating prior cardiac and digestive involvement due to Chagas disease.

article.articleHeadline: El Niño, mosquitoes and low risk perception: specialists urge proactive dengue prevention.
article.articleSummary: El Niño is consolidated with near-certain persistence through February 2027 and expected to reach very strong intensity by year-end, potentially altering temperatures and precipitation and increasing extreme-weather risk. In northern Argentina, Uruguay, and southern Brazil, above-average rainfall and flood risk are anticipated. Dengue transmission is linked to climate trends that shape mosquito habitats; Aedes aegypti, urban-adapted, breeds in water-filled containers around homes. Warmer temperatures speed mosquito development (egg-to-adult in 7–10 days); both heavy rains and drought can create new breeding sites. Argentina experienced its largest dengue outbreak in 2024, with more than half a million cases. Infected travelers can carry the virus in blood, risking local transmission if competent mosquitoes and favorable conditions exist. Prevention combines eliminating breeding sites, covering water storage, using repellents, sustaining surveillance, and seeking early care; vaccination is used where indicated. Dengue has four serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4); prior infection is serotype-specific and a risk factor for severe disease.

article.articleSummary: Poliomyelitis (polio) prevention highlighted by Rotary International's End Polio Now campaign in Pernambuco, Brazil. On Sunday, November 15, 2026, the End Polio Now Cycling Ride will take place in Recife, with a route from Praça de Casa Forte in the North Zone to Praça do Baobá, starting at 8:00. The event emphasizes that vaccination is the only effective protection against polio, a disease worldwide reduced by over 99.9% since 1985. Organizers present the ride as more than a sport activity, serving as a public health awareness effort to keep children's immunizations up to date and to remind communities that polio is preventable. The campaign underscores ongoing eradication efforts and Rotary clubs’ role in Pernambuco to combat poliomyelitis.

article.articleHeadline: Fevers in amphibians and reptiles.
article.articleSummary: Behavioral fever—a rise in body temperature via movement to warmer microhabitats—occurs in amphibians and reptiles when infected. A Brazilian team from the University of São Paulo and Universidade Estadual Paulista analyzed 47 studies published from the 1970s to 2020, comprising 101 measurements in 49 species. They compared healthy and infected individuals, linking field data with high-resolution climate data for wild populations. They found behavioral fever is widespread, with intensity largely explained by local diurnal temperature variation. For every degree of average daily temperature difference, infected animals raised their body temperature by about 0.45°C. Amphibians showed stronger responses than reptiles; bacterial infections yielded clearer increases, while fungal and viral infections were inconclusive. Climate change and landscape changes may reduce thermal heterogeneity, potentially limiting fever-based defenses, and past experiments showed infected lizards died when heat elevation was blocked.

article.articleHeadline: Brazil approves a vaccine against 21 strains of the bacterium behind pneumonia and meningitis.
article.articleSummary: Brazil's ANVISA approved Capvaxive, a 21-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine from MSD, targeting 21 Streptococcus pneumoniae serotypes to prevent invasive pneumococcal disease and pneumonia in adults aged 18+. Approval was published in the Official Journal on the 28th after regulatory review that included input from the U.S. FDA. Capvaxive uses purified polysaccharide capsules conjugated to a carrier protein to elicit antibodies; covered serotypes include 3, 6A, 7F, 8, 9N, 10A, 11A, 12F, 15A, OAc15B, 16F, 17F, 19A, 20A, 22F, 23A, 23B, 24F, 31, 33F, and 35B. Eight serotypes are unique to Capvaxive compared with existing vaccines: 15A, 16F, 23A, 23B, 24F, 31, 35B, OAc15B. Streptococcus pneumoniae can cause otitis media, sinusitis, and invasive disease such as sepsis and meningitis. Phase 3 trials across the Americas, Europe, Asia‑Pacific and Africa enrolled ~8,400 adults; ~5,500 received Capvaxive; age groups: 18–49 (32%), 50–64 (32%), 65–74 (29%), 75+ (8%). Safety demonstrated in adults. In Brazil’s public system (SUS), Capvaxive is not automatically included; Pneumo 20 covers children under 5 and certain priority groups.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue: Tests Help Determine Required Care.
article.articleSummary: As of November 13, 2026, dengue fever, transmitted by Aedes aegypti and caused by four serotypes (DEN-1 to DEN-4), requires rapid diagnostic testing to guide care. In Brazil, clinical staging groups patients as A to D to determine management from outpatient to intensive care; the staging is dynamic. NS1 antigen tests or RT-PCR are preferred in days 1–5 of symptoms, with RT-PCR identifying the circulating serotype. After day 6, serology (IgM/IgG) is recommended. The CBC and serial hematocrit monitor plasma leakage and dehydration risk; leukopenia, lymphocytosis with reactive lymphocytes, and thrombocytopenia are common. Severe dengue (Groups C and D) prompts comprehensive lab assessment: liver (AST/ALT, albumin, bilirubin), pancreatic, renal function, lactate, glucose, cardiac markers (Troponin I, CK-MB), and coagulation studies (PT, aPTT, D-dimer). Differential RT-PCR can detect Zika, Chikungunya, Leptospirosis, Malaria, Influenza, and COVID-19. November 21 marks Brazil’s National Dengue Fight Day.

article.articleHeadline: Parasite affecting horses found for the first time in gray river dolphin.
article.articleSummary: Parasites that cause neurological disease in horses were detected in gray river dolphins off Brazil. In a USP study, 1,103 samples from 159 cetaceans across 21 species found dead or stranded on Brazilian shores (2004–2022) yielded parasites in 14 animals. Sarcocystis neurona was confirmed in two gray river dolphins, with one of them also positive for Toxoplasma gondii. A previously undescribed Sarcocystis lineage was found in six offshore cetaceans—dwarf sperm whale, Cuvier’s beaked whale, Fraser’s dolphin, Atlantic spotted dolphin, and Clymene dolphin—suggesting offshore circulation. Water runoff from land and rivers may transport terrestrial parasites to the ocean; birds could disseminate the offshore lineage. The health impact on the dolphins is unknown, and population-level effects cannot be determined. Sarcocystis neurona is endemic in the Americas and causes equine protozoal myeloencephalitis in horses.

article.articleHeadline: Doctor denounces irregular diagnoses of Hansen's disease in Cuiabá and calls for an investigation by CRM-MT.
article.articleSummary: As of November 13, 2026, Dr. Zeno Augusto alleges irregular Hansen’s disease (leprosy) diagnoses in Cuiabá, Mato Grosso, Brazil, with at least five patients reportedly exposed to questionable assessments. He claims a group of physicians may be acting for commercial gain linked to a compounding pharmacy owned by a mother in Cuiabá, with two doctors and the family participating; one patient diagnosed with Hansen’s disease after fibromyalgia evaluation later found, via a São Paulo biopsy, to have small fiber neuropathy rather than leprosy. He criticizes reliance on neuromodulation, peripheral nerve ultrasound with Doppler, and whole-body thermography as essential for fibromyalgia. The Regional Medical Council of Mato Grosso (CRM-MT) says it will notify the physician to provide details, but no formal investigation or names are established yet; authorities encourage formal complaints through official channels. The case remains unproven pending verification.

article.articleHeadline: Test developed in Rio de Janeiro identifies a fatal disease with just one drop of blood.
article.articleSummary: As of 13 November 2026, researchers in Rio de Janeiro developed a rapid diagnostic test for hantavirus disease that detects infection in 15–20 minutes from a single drop of blood. Created by Fiocruz in collaboration with the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), the assay analyzes cellular and biochemical changes caused by hantavirus. Anvisa approved the technology, enabling production and use across Brazil's health services. With symptoms mimicking influenza or dengue, this test offers earlier and more precise diagnosis to start treatment sooner. Hantavirus disease is transmitted mainly through contact with wild rodents or their excreta (urine, feces, saliva). Incubation is 1–6 weeks; early symptoms include fever, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal, muscular, and head pains. Severe disease may feature red or purple skin spots, gum bleeding, tachycardia, kidney failure, reduced urine output, dry cough, and dyspnea.

article.articleHeadline: Surveillance for zoonotic viruses in human population at the human-animal interface in North Sulawesi, Indonesia
article.articleSummary: Surveillance was conducted in Minahasa District, North Sulawesi, Indonesia, as part of the USAID Emerging Pandemic Threats (EPT) PREDICT project, from November 2017 to December 2018, at Noongan Hospital and Puskesmas Kawangkoan. The study targets high risk populations engaging in wildlife hunting, trade and consumption, in a region with documented wildlife related activities and prior reports of potential zoonotic viruses in bats (henipavirus, filovirus, hantavirus). Objectives: establish baseline data on viruses within selected zoonotic families and identify behavioral risk factors for spillover at the human–wildlife interface. Enrollment included syndromic patients aged >2 years presenting with fever (>38 C) for 24 h to 7 days, including SARI, ILI, fever of unknown origin, encephalitis, or hemorrhagic fever. Biological samples collected: oral/nasal, rectal, blood, urine; stored in TRIzol/VTM and shipped to Eijkman Research Center. Molecular detection by RNA extraction and cDNA synthesis followed prior surveillance protocols to detect viruses within zoonotic families.

article.articleHeadline: Transitional Season Brings Hundreds of Cases of Acute Respiratory Infections and Diarrhea in Bangkalan
article.articleSummary: Acute Respiratory Infections (ISPA) and diarrhea are surging in Bangkalan Regency, East Java, during the transitional season. In week 44 (early November 2026), health authorities reported 679 ISPA cases, 330 diarrhea cases, 270 influenza-like illness (ILI) cases, 146 typhoid, and 144 pneumonia. Head of the Bangkalan Health Department, Dr. Nunuk Kristiani, attributes the ISPA surge to hot, dry air during seasonal change. Prevention emphasizes clean living, complete immunization, regular meals and exercise, adequate water intake, avoiding contact with the sick, and mask use to reduce transmission. Symptoms typically appear about three days after exposure and last 7–10 days, though can persist up to three weeks in some individuals. Residents with cough, fever, runny nose, fatigue, or respiratory distress should seek medical care if symptoms do not improve.

article.articleHeadline: Unpad Lecturer Develops Biosensor for Detecting TB up to Pig DNA
article.articleSummary: Indonesia's Padjadjaran University (Unpad) analytical chemistry lecturer Irkham is developing CRISPR-based electrochemical biosensors to detect infectious diseases and halal-quality markers. In halal-food testing, the sensor detects pork DNA and alcohol to verify products. The approach uses boron-doped diamond electrodes and nanoceria, employing green synthesis methods. Major challenges include ensuring reproducibility and securing investment, while fostering collaborations for broader deployment. Reported from Jakarta on 13 November 2026, the work seeks to expand TB diagnostics and halal verification across Indonesia.

article.articleHeadline: Illegal gold mining pits in East Sumba suspected to have triggered a spike in malaria cases.
article.articleSummary: Illegal gold mining pits in Matawai La Pawu and surrounding areas of East Sumba Regency, Indonesia, are suspected to drive a malaria spike. Abandoned mining holes serve as Anopheles mosquito breeding sites. Preliminary health department findings link most cases to Melolo sub-district (Puskesmas Melolo), which accounts for 56% of malaria in the district. In Umalulu District, 47 malaria cases were found; miners typically stay 4–5 days at the sites and return on weekends, aiding transmission. In 2026, malaria cases total 250, more than five times the 46 cases in 2025, with about 10 positives per 1,000 population on average. After Melolo, the highest counts are in Kambata Mapambuhang and Kananggar, API 7.9 and 6.6 respectively. About 81 miners are spread across several sub-districts. Six elimination priorities are: case finding, epidemiologic investigation, mapping receptive zones and vectors, integrating malaria with maternal and child health programs, migration surveillance, and prevention education.

article.articleHeadline: Visiting a Newborn Baby: Carrying, Kissing, and Selfies Become a Gateway for RSV
article.articleSummary: RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus) poses infection risk to newborns in Jakarta, Indonesia. A physician, Dr. Ulul Albab, warns that common visiting practices—holding, kissing, and selfies with a newborn—can undermine prevention because visitors’ health status is often unknown. Cultural and family expectations in Indonesia make limiting visits difficult; parents risk social judgment for restricting contact. Options such as viewing the baby from behind glass or via video call are mentioned, but not easily accepted culturally. Hand hygiene and cleanliness are hard to enforce at every visit, and airport-style health checks or heavy PPE are not practical for routine family visits. The article emphasizes that protecting newborns can be achieved without forgoing affection: families should balance warmth with cautious interactions, asking visitors to consider the infant’s health before touching or kissing.

article.articleHeadline: Concerned About Tuberculosis Cases in Indonesia, a Surabaya-based Student Creates Health Technology Innovations.
article.articleSummary: Surabaya-based high school student Jonathan Edward Sutadji developed sCODA (Scarcity-aware Constrained Optimization of Dosing Allocation), a health-technology platform to optimize tuberculosis (TB) drug dosing in Indonesia based on available treatment budgets. The 17-year-old Ciputra School Surabaya student built a mathematical model and computer simulation to allocate TB medications efficiently, addressing Indonesia’s persistent TB burden. He extracted laboratory data from TB time-kill assays published by ERA4TB and used regression analysis to fit Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth kinetics against isoniazid. The optimization system then simulates multiple regimens to identify dosing combinations that maximize therapeutic impact within budget. sCODA earned two international awards in 2026: World Science, Environment and Engineering Competition (Jakarta, Aug 11–14) and the International Science and Invention Fair (ISIF) (UI, Depok, Oct 12–17).

article.articleHeadline: Social Stigma and Family Dynamics Shape Tuberculosis Care Delays in West
article.articleSummary: West Java, Indonesia—A qualitative descriptive study at the DOTS clinic of RSUD dr. Slamet in Garut interviewed nine TB outpatients (seven female, two male, 18–42 years). Delays in help-seeking and treatment non-adherence were driven more by the social meanings of tuberculosis, stigma (including aib), and family dynamics than by knowledge gaps, with structural barriers such as mandatory digital registration worsening access. Early TB symptoms were often normalized; extrapulmonary signs were rarely linked to TB, and healthcare experiences featured fragmented diagnostics and inconsistent communication. Family relationships emerged as the most influential factor, with six participants noting their impact on adherence. Medication fatigue, ongoing fear, and distress from clinical interactions further hindered adherence. Participants used self-monitoring strategies like cautionary witnessing to learn from peers who stopped treatment. The authors urge family-inclusive, stigma-reducing, patient-centered programs and proactive self-monitoring tools from treatment onset.

article.articleSummary: Measles vaccination campaign targets more than 40,000 children aged 9 months to 15 years in Shabunda Rural Health Zone, South Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Launched 7 November 2026 for 25 days, the effort—supported by MSF Spain—seeks to boost protection and reach those who missed doses during previous campaigns or routine services. The campaign combines measles vaccination with screening for malaria and malnutrition; children testing positive receive immediate care through the health zone and partners. Two operating modes are used: fixed-post vaccination within health facilities and an outreach strategy to bring services to remote communities. Dr. Guillaume Kiatughu, medical chief of the Shabunda Rural Health Zone, says this combined approach expands coverage and reduces measles transmission. Health authorities urge parents to vaccinate, highlighting immunization as essential for preventing vaccine-preventable diseases and improving child health.

article.articleHeadline: DRC: Anticipating the Impact of Interventions Against Measles and Cholera - ACP
article.articleSummary: Kinshasa, 13 November 2026 - An expert workshop in Kinshasa, DRC, focused on epidemiological modeling to anticipate the impact of interventions against measles and cholera under the Gates Foundation-supported Orcas project. Led by INRB's epidemiological modeling unit, the event brings together DSE, PEV, and PNECO to identify operational questions that models can answer to reverse the epidemic curve and reduce measles and cholera cases. The consortium includes Redeemer's University (Nigeria), University of Oxford (UK), and Nigeria's NCDC. Outcomes include stakeholder mapping, data-source inventory, and defined modeling questions to guide predictive tools. Planned decision-support resources will include an analysis platform, policy briefs, and situation reports for decision-makers. Methodologically, the team will blend mechanistic mathematical modeling with AI, leveraging Google's population-dynamics models and neural networks to forecast hotspots and case trajectories, incorporating climate, flood, and mobility data, especially in eastern DRC.

article.articleSummary: During a visit to Bunia, UNICEF's Associate Director for Health Emergencies, Dr. Douglas Noble, commended progress in combating the seventeenth Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ituri region. After meeting military governor General Gaby Kasongo Mulumba, Noble emphasised continued collaboration with Congolese authorities to eradicate the outbreak. UNICEF support spans hygiene installations in schools and rural areas, specialized training, and prevention-kit distribution, with logistics delivering to Bunia substantial supplies including more than half a billion metric tons of PPE and medical equipment. The agency has trained over 1,000 community health actors to boost household risk-communication, enhanced active case finding, and ensured drinking-water access in health facilities and schools. Border controls include temperature checks, thermal cameras, and rigorous medical testing overseen by the hygiene service, but the strategy faces local opposition, with politicians such as Luc Malembe criticizing geographic fairness and economic impact while not fully halting viral movement to enclaves. Reopening will depend on a clear reversal in the outbreak’s trajectory in the epicenter and the ability of medical teams to bend the curve.

article.articleHeadline: Dispute over the "Hope" in the Ebola epidemic.
article.articleSummary: WHO is testing three vaccines against Bundibugyo Ebola virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo amid an outbreak. The Tumaini platform, launched in late October and led by Kinshasa’s INRB with the University of Antwerp, uses Merck’s Ervebo (rVSV-ZEBOV) as the lead. The Phase 2/3 study allocates about 20,000 Ervebo doses to evaluate safety, dosing, and efficacy in contacts of infected individuals. Design: one group receives an immediate dose; controls get a placebo; all participants receive Ervebo on day 29. First results aren’t expected before early 2027. Ituri, with over four million people across 66 health centers, spans eight provinces with dozens of outbreaks. MSF’s BRAVO vaccinates up to 20,000 health workers to assess protection. WHO warns mass vaccination could overwhelm the health system and boost hesitancy; 50,000 doses are reserved for medical staff outside the trial. Merck should release doses to a global stockpile; wealthy nations should avoid hoarding.

article.articleHeadline: DRC: In Oicha, the Ebola treatment center lacks space for about thirty patients - Mali Actu
article.articleSummary: In Oicha, North Kivu, DRC, the Ebola treatment center at the Oicha General Referral Hospital is overcrowded, hosting about thirty patients. Rooms are shared by three: two sleeping on mats on the floor and one on a bed, without mosquito nets. The ETC occupies a former transit facility used in 2018 during the tenth Ebola outbreak. Dr. Melchi Lukumbola says confirmed cases rose rapidly, exceeding the initial capacity of ten beds for confirmed and ten for suspected, prompting the addition of tents. The hospital also opened new rooms for suspected cases awaiting laboratory results. Officials are calling for urgent construction of a properly-equipped Ebola treatment center with sufficient capacity.

article.articleHeadline: Africa: floods, famine, and diseases... the UN warns of a humanitarian catastrophe threatening millions of people.
article.articleSummary: UN agencies warn Africa faces a humanitarian catastrophe driven by floods, famine and disease, with East Africa’s heavy rains causing displacement and heightened infectious-disease risks as well as a slow global fight against tuberculosis. In Somalia, some 170,000 people have been affected by floods; over 2,400 homes destroyed, about 5,900 damaged, 70 schools and 55 health facilities hit, and roughly 5,300 cattle lost. Burundi reports floods affecting over 46,000 people with many displaced and significant damage to schools and farmland. Kenya and Rwanda record displacement and fatalities; Tanzania experiences floods and landslides (1 death, 7 injuries). Ethiopia and South Sudan face droughts, with about 3.9 million Ethiopians needing emergency food and 1.83 million requiring WASH support. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, some 29 million people face a food-security crisis, with aid anticipated through early 2027, including Kinshasa and other regions per IPC-WFP-FAO-Unicef assessments.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Beni: acceptance of the disease and barrier measures to overcome fear - ACP
article.articleSummary: Ebola is ongoing in eight provinces, including Beni in North Kivu, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, as of 13 November 2026. Stigma around Ebola Treatment Centers (CTEs) is criticized; CTEs are described as care spaces, with quality defined by disease stage and lab confirmation. Families should regularly visit to provide moral support, reassure patients that they are not abandoned, and show care teams’ efforts to counter rumors.

article.articleHeadline: Democratic Republic of the Congo - Myths, Microphones and Medicine: Child broadcasters use radio to tackle Ebola
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, declared 15 May in Ituri Province, eastern DRC, has spread to 67 health zones across eight provinces with over 11,000 infections and more than 5,300 deaths, about a quarter among children, making it the largest Ebola outbreak in DRC and the second largest globally. The broadcasts explain how Ebola spreads, how to prevent infection, symptoms to look for, and where to seek help, countering myths and fear. The initiative promotes trust and protective behaviors, including regular handwashing and safe handling of the deceased, while schools stay safer and communities report symptoms promptly.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in the DRC: 12.5 tonnes of prevention supplies delivered to N'Djili International Airport, to the Ministry of Health, to the police, and to CHU50 by the Angel Foundation
article.articleSummary: Ebola remains active in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus—the 17th outbreak in the country. As of 11 November 2026, INSP reports 11,197 confirmed cases and 5,471 deaths (case fatality rate 48.9%), across eight provinces and 68 health zones. Production occurs at Guoguang Biotech's Tanzi Plant in Taichung using an advanced bioreactor process, with annual capacity of at least 1 million doses for Taiwan and ASEAN. The vaccine targets active immunization for children aged 2 months to under 6 years, with an efficacy of 99.21%.

article.articleHeadline: 'Coronavirus might be evolving': Professor Suresh V Kuchipudi
article.articleSummary: Coronavirus may still be circulating in animals, warns Suresh V Kuchipudi of the University of Pittsburgh. In U.S. white-tailed deer, infection is widespread; the original strain has circulated for more than four years and has changed significantly, potentially escaping more than 70% of antibody protection while still infecting humans and deer. Genomic surveillance of human cases has largely stopped, suggesting the virus could be evolving unseen. The concern extends to H5N1 bird flu, now found in birds and animals on every continent and in dairy cattle in America; each spillover from birds to mammals moves the virus closer to human adaptation. Nipah outbreaks recur in a northern pocket of Kerala (Keralam); cases are picked up only when infections reach hospitals, implying local exposure patterns. Policymakers and scientists should study local conditions and monitor evolving threats.

Preventive guidance for Hyderabad residents includes wearing masks outdoors, frequent hand washing, avoiding public places with fever, ensuring ventilation with outdoor air, and adequate sleep. Do not shake hands, reuse tissues, or touch mouth/eyes, and consult doctors before self-medicating.

article.articleHeadline: Plague deaths in India have significantly decreased - WHO information.
article.articleSummary: WHO data show plague deaths in India have fallen sharply since 2015; India’s plague mortality rate dropped from 28 per lakh in 2015 to 18 per lakh in 2025, a 38% decline, surpassing the global average reduction of 35%. Under Prime Minister Modi’s leadership, the campaign has become a mass movement: since 2024, 25 crore people have been screened for plague, about 11 crore X-ray scans performed, and 48.64 lakh cases detected and started on treatment. This consolidation reflects a strong treatment infrastructure and sustained government support toward a plague-free India.

article.articleHeadline: Scoping Review Maps Pathogen Frequencies in Acute Undifferentiated Fever
article.articleSummary: Dengue, malaria, scrub typhus, leptospirosis, enteric fever, and non-scrub rickettsioses drive acute undifferentiated febrile illness (AUFI) in India, per a scoping review of 90 studies published up to Nov 9, 2024. Dengue appeared in 63 studies, malaria in 30, leptospirosis in 28, scrub typhus in 27, enteric fever in 21, and non-scrub rickettsioses in 4. Among 28 broad-panel AUFI studies, dengue led in 13, scrub typhus in 7, malaria in 4, leptospirosis in 3, and enteric fever in 1. Median pathogen proportions were higher in pathogen-directed studies for malaria (32.1% vs 8.6%), scrub typhus (20.0% vs 12.5%), and leptospirosis (17.2% vs 6.2%), with dengue similar across designs (25.3% vs 27.5%). Diagnostic approaches varied: dengue frequently used high-certainty NS1/molecular tests (47/63), while scrub typhus and leptospirosis often relied on serology (20/27; 23/28). The study highlights geographic, design, and diagnostic heterogeneity and maps selected infections rather than a complete national etiologic picture.

article.articleHeadline: River Confluence Microbes Show Complex Genomic Potential During Mass
article.articleSummary: At the Sangam confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna in Prayagraj, India, the Mahakumbh pilgrimage triggers episodic perturbations of river microbiota, with major inputs of organic matter, nutrients, pharmaceuticals, personal-care products, fecal material, and skin microbes from upstream runoff. 16S rRNA sequencing shows baseline dominance of Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, and Bacteroidetes, including Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Bacillus, Aeromonas, and Streptomyces; during mass bathing, blooms of Escherichia, Klebsiella, and Vibrio appear, with metal-tolerant taxa rising. Pre-event BOD is 2.37 mg/L, rising to ~6.37 mg/L during the festival and about 4.93 mg/L post-event; earlier festivals reported BOD 14 mg/L, COD 67 mg/L, ammonium 2.15 mg/L, and a ~130-fold biomass increase with 792 and 482 MPN/100 mL for total and fecal coliforms. COD peaks near 30 mg/L; pH shifts from 8.17 to 8.53, then 8.33; DO declines with respiration. The review defines genomic resilience as a population’s capacity to maintain or recover function after disturbance via genetic or regulatory changes, and distinguishes it from resistance, acclimation, and adaptation. An observational ecogenomic framework is proposed, noting many taxa are freshwater natives and source attribution remains unresolved.

article.articleHeadline: China Sustains Over 99.6 Percent Hepatitis B Mother-to-Child Prevention
article.articleSummary: China reports nationwide hepatitis B PMTCT success >99.6% from 2023–2025, based on 569,730 infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers across 31 provinces. Antenatal screening remained ~99.94–99.95%, with birth‑dose vaccination plus 100 IU hepatitis B immunoglobulin within 12 hours, subsequent vaccines at 1 and 6 months, and maternal antiviral prophylaxis for eligible women; post‑vaccination serology occurs at 7–12 months. Prevention success was 99.73% (2023), 99.66% (2024), and 99.68% (2025). Pediatric HBV infection among screened children declined from 9.09 to 7.52 to 2.92 per 100,000 live births. Among residual infections, 37.77% produced anti‑HBs, indicating serological heterogeneity. Regional infection rates remained higher in the western region (11.69→8.80→3.52 per 100,000), with central (7.70→7.64→3.06) and eastern (8.42→6.48→2.37) also showing declines. Findings support progress toward WHO 2030 HBV elimination targets; Maldives achieved triple elimination by May 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Study Uncovers Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis Mutations and Lineage Patterns
article.articleSummary: In Shantou, China, 148 Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates collected in 2024 show substantial drug resistance. Phenotypic resistance to at least one drug occurred in 31.8% of isolates, while 98.6% harbored detectable resistance mutations across analyzed loci. Isoniazid resistance was most common (20.9%), followed by streptomycin (10.1%), with rifampicin and ethambutol each at 6.2%. Retreated cases (20.4% of samples) exhibited significantly higher resistance than newly diagnosed cases (p<0.05). Genetic analysis found katG Arg463Leu in 66.2% and gyrA Ser95Thr in 98.0% of strains. Genotyping via IS6110 and 8-locus MIRU-VNTR differentiated 134 genotypes with a 9.46% overall clustering rate. Lineage 2 dominated; resistance mutations localized to inhA, rpsL, rrs, and pncA within this lineage. Phylogeny and mutation patterns align with Erdman and CDC1551 references. Methods included Löwenstein-Jensen DST, PCR/SnapGene, and MEGA11 phylogeny; Fisher’s exact and chi-squared tests assessed associations.

article.articleHeadline: Pastoral Case Series Details HIV and Brucellosis Coinfection Management in
article.articleSummary: Seven consecutive male people living with HIV (PWH) with laboratory-confirmed Brucella infection were treated at the Fourth People’s Hospital of Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, northwest China, from July 2021 to May 2025. All had pastoral exposure to sheep or cattle. Presentations combined fever, fatigue, night sweats, with focal lesions (two with lumbar spondylitis/spondylodiscitis; two with epididymo-orchitis/hydroceles; four with testicular fluid collections). Antibacterial regimens plus antiretroviral therapy produced clinical improvement or stabilization in all, with no microbiologically confirmed recurrences during up to 54 months of follow-up. Brucellosis in China reached 62,055 cases in 2024 (4.41/100,000; ~90% northern). Ningxia reported rising local incidence (2022: 86.76/100k; 2023: 63.17; 2024: 34.81; 2,538 cases). Brucella melitensis was the predominant species. Diagnosis relied on culture or tube agglutination ≥1:100; four patients had positive blood cultures; six had agglutination titers 1:100–1:800; one culture-positive but agglutination-negative in an immunocompromised host.

article.articleHeadline: Severe Scrub Typhus Triggers Multi-Organ Failure Without Classic Eschar in
article.articleSummary: Severe scrub typhus (tsutsugamushi disease) triggered life-threatening systemic inflammation and multi-organ failure in a 47-year-old Shenzhen chef without a diagnostic eschar. Orientia tsutsugamushi, transmitted by chigger mites, causes tsutsugamushi disease, endemic across the Asia–Pacific including southern China, with ~1 million infections annually and rising Guangdong incidence. The patient developed acute respiratory distress syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hepatic injury, and myocardial damage after an unrecognized arthropod bite. He presented after ten days of fever and myalgia; on admission he had SOFA 7, severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 70→33×10^9/L), PaO2/FiO2 ~165, CRP 102.61 mg/L, D-dimer >20 mg/L FEU, and prolonged aPTT 48.9 s with DIC features. ALT 216 U/L and bilirubin 30.9 μmol/L indicated hepatic injury; ARDS met Berlin criteria. Murine typhus and dengue were considered but eschar absence complicated recognition. The case, treated at Peking University Shenzhen Hospital in June 2024, underscores eschar-negative scrub typhus in China.

article.articleHeadline: China's first domestically produced chikungunya virus antigen test kit approved for market; a rapid screening tool debuts.
article.articleSummary: China has approved the first domestically produced chikungunya virus antigen test kit for market, introducing a rapid on-site screening tool for grassroots clinics and border ports. The assay uses colloidal gold immunochromatography, requiring only a sample and producing a visually readable result in 15–30 minutes without specialized equipment, and it can be stored at room temperature. This enables immediate screening and clinical support, bolstering vector-borne disease surveillance and early response in the Greater Bay Area. The kit is developed by DaAn Gene (Zhongshan) Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of Guangzhou DaAn Gene Co., under Guangzhou Pharmaceutical Group’s indirect control since 2026. DaAn Gene’s broader diagnostic portfolio includes hepatitis, HIV, syphilis, EBV, and influenza, underscoring enhanced public health supply chains and regional diagnostic capacity.

article.articleHeadline: Study Uncovers Microbial Risks in Takeaway Salads Despite Consumer
article.articleSummary: China’s Jinan City, Shandong Province, a mixed-methods study found microbial contamination, not pesticide residues, is the primary post-harvest hazard for ready-to-eat salads. The survey of 349 consumers—predominantly urban women aged 21–30 with bachelor’s degrees—showed pesticide residues as the top safety concern, followed by microbial contamination. Lab analyses of commercially sold salads found pesticides largely undetectable (two weak positives in round lettuce) but pronounced bacterial contamination across channels. On purchase day, aerobic plate counts exceeded 5 log CFU/g in takeout and supermarket salads; E. coli exceeded limits in takeout and rose during five days of 4°C storage. Online/e-commerce salads stayed within guidelines. Household decontamination regimens (10-minute tap rinse vs 10-minute 1% sodium bicarbonate soak plus rinse) were evaluated, with initial contamination varying by produce type. Trust in processors was lower than trust in farm producers, and safety concerns correlated with purchasing choices when supply chains lack transparency.

article.articleHeadline: Guangdong Identified as Primary Origin of HIV-1 Introductions to Haikou
article.articleSummary: Guangdong is identified as the primary external source of HIV-1 introductions into Haikou, China, across four major subtypes (CRF07_BC, CRF01_AE, CRF65_cpx, CRF55_01B). In a 2021–2024 study of 1,125 pol sequences plus a cross-sectional field survey, CRF07_BC (38.6%) and CRF01_AE (35.6%) were most prevalent; local clustering was 33.6% (CRF07_BC), 36.7% (CRF01_AE), 54.9% (CRF55_01B), and 86.4% (CRF65_cpx). Bayesian relaxed clock and Skygrid phylogeography placed Guangdong as the primary source for all four subtypes; Beijing contributed CRF01_AE_C1 and CRF65_cpx, Shanghai CRF07_BC. Within Hainan, CRF01_AE showed bidirectional spread between Haikou and Sanya/Dongfang; CRF07_BC and CRF65_cpx spread from Haikou to six other cities. Field data from 451 participants found 52.3% acquired HIV outside Haikou; Guangdong accounted for 16.95% of externals (40 cases), with Sanya driving internal cases (18, 7.63%). The findings support cross-regional prevention for mobile populations.

article.articleHeadline: Liu Huan's cause of death revealed for the first time: septic shock, after more than a decade battling bladder cancer — how dangerous is bladder cancer?
article.articleSummary: Liu Huan, a noted musician, died on September 25, 2026, from septic (infectious) shock after a prolonged battle with bladder cancer. Diagnosed in 2012, he experienced a recurrence in 2017 and refused radical cystectomy to keep his bladder, continuing treatment for nearly a decade. By late 2025, cancer had metastasized, and in 2026 he underwent multiple lines of therapy in Shanghai, including Enfortumab Vedotin plus Pembrolizumab (an antibody-drug conjugate with a PD-1 inhibitor). Lung metastases briefly shrank, but he developed severe enteritis and infection leading to septic shock. He was laid to rest in Beijing near the Great Wall; his wife Lu Lu released a public letter. The article notes bladder cancer’s high recurrence and progression risk, with smoking and aromatic amine exposure as major risk factors, and emphasizes painless hematuria as a key symptom and the role of surveillance and possible cystectomy for high-risk cases.

article.articleHeadline: Rodents in Southwestern Shanxi Show High Prevalence of Diverse Bartonella
article.articleSummary: Small rodents from Yuncheng City, southwestern Shanxi Province, China, show high Bartonella prevalence and genetic diversity. Among 106 trapped animals, 49 (46.23%) tested positive for Bartonella DNA (95% CI 36.58–55.87%). Seven rodent species were captured; Apodemus agrarius was most numerous (59). Liver, spleen, and kidney tissues were screened by real-time PCR targeting ssrA; overall tissue differences were significant (P=0.03), but pairwise contrasts were not significant after Bonferroni correction. No significant associations were found with sex, habitat (forest vs farmland), or sampling site. Phylogenetic analysis of gltA sequences identified seven Bartonella taxa from 41 sequences, led by Bartonella grahamii (17), followed by Candidatus Bartonella rudakovii (5), B. fuyuanensis (5), B. queenslandensis (4), B. taylorii (4), B. phoceensis (3), and one unclassified lineage (3). B. grahamii was predominant and comprised four haplotypes; Apodemus agrarius carried four haplotypes (Hd = 0.745 ± 0.098).

article.articleHeadline: BFAR warns vs eating shellfish from 4 Eastern Visayas bays
article.articleSummary: Paralytic shellfish toxins linked to red tide were detected in shellfish from four Eastern Visayas bays, prompting BFAR-8 to issue a Nov. 12 advisory prohibiting gathering, selling, and consumption of all shellfish, including Acetes (alamang), from Carigara Bay (Leyte: Babatngon, San Miguel, Capoocan, Barugo, Carigara), Irong-Irong Bay (Samar: Catbalogan City), Matarinao Bay (Eastern Samar: General MacArthur, Quinapondan, Hernani, Salcedo), and Cambatutay Bay (Tarangnan, Samar). Local red tide warning issued for Cambatutay Bay while confirmatory tests are awaited from the BFAR National Fisheries Laboratory Division using the Receptor Binding Assay. Shellfish toxins include saxitoxin causing paralytic shellfish poisoning with numbness, tingling, difficulty breathing, and potentially death; cooking does not destroy the toxin. The advisory notes fish, squid, shrimp and crabs from these sites remain safe if fresh and gutted of internal organs and thoroughly washed. BFAR continues coastal monitoring.

article.articleHeadline: Tshwane residents urged to watch for malaria symptoms as Gauteng cases rise
article.articleSummary: Malaria in Gauteng, South Africa, prompts intensified alerts in Tshwane as cases rise. By end of September, Gauteng recorded 17 malaria deaths; 17 fatalities this year had travel histories to malaria-endemic areas. Mozambique accounted for 59% of the province’s malaria deaths. In 2025, Gauteng had 666 malaria cases and seven deaths; by September 2026, 768 cases and 17 deaths, a 38.6% year-on-year increase. Common symptoms include headaches, body aches, weakness, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Travel histories indicate imported risk, with 15 of 17 fatalities having travelled to Southern African Development Community (SADC) countries. Health authorities urge travellers to visit travel clinics and take precautions before and after travel; outreach at taxi ranks and bus stations targets high-risk travellers during holidays. La Niña-driven flooding has boosted regional malaria across DRC, Mozambique, Angola, Tanzania, Zimbabwe, Malawi, Zambia, Madagascar, Comoros, and parts of South Africa (Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal), Namibia, Botswana.

article.articleHeadline: Africa CDC: Ebola cases top 11,145 with 5,437 deaths at six months
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak across Africa has 11,145 confirmed infections and 5,437 deaths at six months, with 3,058 recoveries (case fatality 48.8 per cent). Most challenges are in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where insecurity and weak contact tracing hinder response; only about 11 per cent of new cases are linked to known contacts (target 95 per cent), highlighting operational gaps and a strained health system amid conflict and displacement. Kenya reports nine cases and two deaths, with the first imported on October 6; the last Ebola patient has been discharged and the final 11 contacts completed 21‑day monitoring, with no new cases since October 19. Nigeria identifies 62 contacts; 59 have completed monitoring, three remain under monitoring. Ten other African nations are designated high‑risk: South Sudan, Rwanda, Zambia, Central African Republic, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, Republic of the Congo, Burundi, Somalia. Africa CDC declared a public health emergency of continental security on May 18, following the WHO declaring a PHEIC.

article.articleHeadline: Programmatic Study Tracks Mortality in Zambian Patients with Drug-Resistant
article.articleSummary: Zambia-based retrospective cohort study of adults co-infected with drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) and HIV, using National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Programme records from 2018–2022 across all ten provinces. Among 655 participants with documented outcomes, mortality was 11.0% (72 deaths). Median age 37 years; 62.4% male. DR-TB defined as Mycobacterium tuberculosis resistant to at least one anti-TB drug. A complete-case multivariable analysis (n=127) found higher mortality with brief treatment interruption (adjusted risk ratio [aRR] 10.18; 95% CI 2.18–47.46; p=0.003), alcohol consumption (aRR 7.16; 95% CI 1.29–39.70; p=0.019), and female sex (aRR 4.63; 95% CI 1.07–20.09; p=0.040). Sensitivity analysis excluding alcohol use changed significance, with hospital admission and pallor emerging as factors. Authors note substantial missing data, rendering complete-case findings exploratory and call for longitudinal research. Programmatic recommendations include enhanced treatment adherence, routine alcohol screening, and closer monitoring for hospitalized patients and those with pallor to mitigate mortality.

article.articleHeadline: Nakhon Ratchasima Public Health Office warns raw-food eaters! Beware of Ear Deafness Fever. In 2026 there have been 76 cases and 9 deaths.
article.articleSummary: Streptococcus suis infection linked to pork is causing illness in Nakhon Ratchasima Province, Thailand. From Jan 1 to Nov 11, 2026, Nakhon Ratchasima reported 76 cases and 9 deaths, the highest in Health Zone 9; neighboring provinces Chaiyaphum 27, Buriram 25, Surin 15. Cumulative incidence is 2.75 per 100,000, below the 3-year median of 3.90 (99 cases, 9 deaths). Over 2567–2569, 122 cases/8 deaths; 87/13; 76/9. Transmission occurs via consumption of raw or undercooked pork or pork blood, and contact with pig tissues through broken skin or mucous membranes. Symptoms include fever, chills, body aches, severe headache, vomiting, neck stiffness, and ear fullness or hearing loss; severe cases may progress to meningitis, sepsis, endocarditis, deafness, or death. Prevention emphasizes avoiding raw pork, separating raw/cooked utensils, buying from reputable sources, and protective hygiene for workers; seek care promptly if symptoms develop.

article.articleHeadline: Diphtheria in Thailand 2026
article.articleSummary: 61 suspected diphtheria cases in Thailand (Jan 1–Nov 9, 2026) with 8 deaths (case-fatality 13%), age 8 months–82 years (median 18; highest in children <4; male:female 1.14:1). Narathiwat reports 10 cases; southern border provinces and four Songkhla districts account for 21 cases and 5 deaths, 3 lab-confirmed; no nationwide outbreak, but continued risk. Diphtheria spreads via coughing/sneezing or contact with secretions; incubation 2–5 days; symptoms include fever, sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and a grayish-white throat membrane; severe cases can cause airway obstruction and cardiac or nervous-system complications. DDC is increasing surveillance, contact tracing, and readiness of diphtheria antitoxin; expanding vaccination access, especially in the south. Vaccination: five-dose series at 2,4,6 months with boosters at 18 months and 4 years; school-age boosters; adults should receive dT boosters. Parents should check records and seek care for suspicious symptoms; mask and hygiene measures advised.

article.articleHeadline: GHS launches second round of MDA against Onchocerciasis
article.articleSummary: Ghana Health Service launches the second round of its 2026 Mass Drug Administration (MDA) against Onchocerciasis (river blindness) from November 15–29 across 86 endemic districts in 15 regions, with free medication for eligible residents delivered by health workers and community drug distributors. Onchocerciasis, a parasite transmitted by infected blackflies, can damage skin and eyes and cause blindness, impairing work, schooling and livelihoods. Since interventions began in 1997, districts requiring treatment have fallen from 152 to 86. The first round (June 20–July 10) treated over 4.8 million people with 86.1% national coverage. Household registration gaps are a challenge; registration will be strengthened under Free Primary Healthcare and supervision improved. Noor Dubai FoundationMais (Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives) provides US$7.7 million for a three-year program—twice-yearly MDA, surveillance, and training—aiming to exceed 5 million people treated annually and US$410 million in economic benefits over 30 years, with elimination targeted by 2030. In Round 1, about 4.7 million across 86 districts were treated and 20,000 trained. The campaign emphasizes media collaboration and continued partner support.
